0115.event: At Clacton in England, about four hundred fifty thousand years ago, a spear tip of yew wood came out of the ancient shore, shaped by hand and hardened in fire. The hunters were arming themselves with more than stone now. Wood could fly straight and true, thrown or thrust, and the forest gave its weapons freely. The yew has a spring in it, and the point was balanced to that spring. After the spear, the hunt was never the same. The distance grew, the danger shrank, and the scales tipped toward the hunters. Four hundred fifty thousand years of flight began with a shaped stick, and we have been throwing ever since.
0115.announce: A spear-cast song from the old shore: The Clacton Spear.
0115.title: The Clacton Spear
0115.piece:
Yew wood, shaped by hand and fire,
the spear was the hunters' desire.
Throw it far, or thrust it true.
The forest gives its best to you.
The point is balanced, keen and straight.
The hunt will never more wait
on stone alone. The wood can fly.
The spear was born to split the sky.
Four hundred fifty thousand years
of flight, of hopes, of hunter's fears
laid down. The distance grew that day.
We throw the spear the same old way.
The yew still springs in the strong hand.
The spear still flies across the land.

0116.event: From the Pit of Bones in Spain comes a skull laid down about four hundred thirty thousand years ago that tells a quieter story than the shaft around it. A terrible blow had cracked it, and then, slowly, the bone knit and healed. Someone survived. And survival like that seems unlikely alone. While the wound closed, someone may have fed the wounded one, watched the long doubtful days, and kept a place soft for healing. The mended skull is proof of more than medicine. It is proof of patience, of a community that waited. The scar says what we still say: we do not leave our wounded. We mend them.
0116.announce: A healing verse for the wounded one: The Mended Skull.
0116.title: The Mended Skull
0116.piece:
A blow fell hard. The skull was cracked.
The pain was deep. The future blacked.
But hands, it seems, were there to tend,
to wait beside, to be a friend
through the long days of doubt and ache,
till the bone began its slow remake.
The skull knit. The wound grew whole.
The healing touched the very soul
of the band. They may not have turned away.
They may have kept the wounded, day by day.
Four hundred thirty thousand years.
The scar remains. The love appears
in bone, in patience, in the wait.
We mend our own. We never hate
the broken. We make them strong.
The mending has been ours so long.

0117.event: In Qesem Cave in the Levant, about four hundred twenty thousand years ago, the hearths burn in the center of the living floor, not at the edge but at the very heart of the home. Fire was kept here daily, like a lamp never let go out, fed morning, noon, and night. The cave became a house around that flame: the center that held the band, the light that never departed. The firekeepers knew the art of the never-ending: keep it small, keep it bright, and never let it die. Four hundred twenty thousand years of tending, and the lesson is the same. Someone has to stay and feed it. Someone always did.
0117.announce: The lamp that never went out, in song: The Qesem Firekeepers.
0117.title: The Qesem Firekeepers
0117.piece:
In the center of the cave it burns,
the flame that never dies, but turns
the dark to home, the cold to warm.
The firekeepers' endless charm:
feed it morning, noon, and night.
Keep it small. Keep it bright.
Four hundred twenty thousand years
of tending, through the hopes and fears.
The lamp that never went out still glows
in every hearth the keeper knows.
Sit close. The center holds us all.
We answer the fire's quiet call.
The cave is home because it burns.
The flame returns. The flame returns.

0118.event: At Schoeningen in Germany, about four hundred thousand years ago, eight spears of spruce lie beside butchered horses where the hunt ended. The spears are balanced like modern javelins, weighted forward, tapered and smooth, made to fly true. This was no lucky strike. It was the planned advance: the ambush at the lakeshore, the thrown spear, the coordinated drive. The weapon was already art, and the hunt was already a battle plan. Hold one in the mind's hand, and the craftsman's pride is still there, four hundred thousand years later. The first true weapons were not found. They were made, and the making changed everything.
0118.announce: Eight spears in flight, a verse: The Schoeningen Spears.
0118.title: The Schoeningen Spears
0118.piece:
Eight spears of spruce, balanced true,
weighted forward, smooth to you
who hold them. Feel the craftsman's pride.
Four hundred thousand years wide
the gap, yet the hand still knows
the balance that the javelin throws.
Beside the horses where they fell,
the spears have their tale to tell:
no chance, no luck, but plan and art,
the ambush, and the hunter's heart.
The lakeshore was the chosen ground.
The spears flew straight without a sound
of doubt. The first true weapons, made,
not found. The hunt was no more afraid.

0119.event: In Germany, about four hundred thousand years ago, the ribs of butchered horses bear marks that match the great spruce spears: the planned hunt, written in bone. It was an ambush at the lakeshore, the herd driven to the water, the spears in flight, the water churning white. This was perhaps not chaos. It may have been the oldest battle plan: the trap, the timing, the hunters moving as one. Stand among them in the mind's eye, and the coordination is startling. They were not a mob. They were a crew, and the hunt had made them true. Four hundred thousand years later, every team that moves as one is their heir.
0119.announce: Thunder on the lakeshore, in a hunting verse: The Horse Hunt.
0119.title: The Horse Hunt
0119.piece:
The ribs bear marks the spears have made.
The plan was laid. The trap was laid.
Drive the herd to the lakeshore's edge.
The water churns. The hunters pledge
as one to move, as one to throw.
The spears fly straight. The horses know
too late. Perhaps it was not chaos, but art,
the oldest battle plan, the hunter's heart.
Four hundred thousand years, the shore,
the thunder of the hooves no more,
but in the bone the story stays:
we hunted well in those old days.
The crew moved one. The plan was true.
The hunt made hunters out of you.

0120.event: In England, about four hundred thousand years ago, long thin blades struck from prepared cores begin to appear: not the chunky chopper, not the teardrop's weight, but something slender and straight. The core was prepared first, shaped with care, and then the blade was struck from it in one clean blow. It foreshadowed a revolution. The planning had moved before the strike: the mind's outline in flint, the design before the deed. Hold one up to the light, and the future is in it, keen and bright. Four hundred thousand years ago, we started making with the mind, not just the hand, and the edge has never been the same.
0120.announce: A thin-edge verse for the coming craft: The First Long Blades.
0120.title: The First Long Blades
0120.piece:
Long and thin, from the prepared core,
the blades are coming. Never before
such slender edges, straight and keen.
The future in the flint is seen.
Prepare the core with patient art.
Then strike, and let the blade depart
in one clean blow. The mind designs
before the hand the flint refines.
Four hundred thousand years, the start
of making with the mind and heart
together. The long blades whisper: more
is coming. Knock on the future's door.
The edge will never be the same.
We make the blade. We make the name.

0121.event: In East Africa, about three hundred eighty thousand years ago, the fossils tell a quiet argument. Brains are getting bigger, and teeth are getting smaller, and the two changes may point to one cause: cooking. Fire had started doing the chewing first, softening the meat and roots before they ever reached the mouth. Smaller jaws were enough, and the energy saved went to the brain, which burst its ancient bounds. Sit beside that old flame in the mind's eye, and watch the meal go soft. We told nature to do the work for us, and fire obliged. The cooking change may have helped make us human, one softened meal at a time.
0121.announce: A fireside tale of the softened meal: The Cooking Change.
0121.title: The Cooking Change
0121.piece:
The old ones sat around the flame,
and watched the meat go soft, the same
old hunger fed a gentler way.
The fire had learned to chew that day.
The jaws grew small. The brains grew wide.
The cooked meal turned the ancient tide.
Three hundred eighty thousand years.
The fire dried the ancient tears
of hunger. Soft food, big minds.
The hardest work the flame unbinds.
We told the fire: do the chewing.
And it did. And we kept stewing
our way to who we are today.
The cooking change is here to stay.
The meal that made us, warm and deep,
we eat, and then we fall asleep,
and dream the dreams the fire gave.
The flame's our oldest, kindest friend.

0122.event: On the Atlantic coast of France, about three hundred sixty thousand years ago, a stone-lined hearth sits at the very edge of the western world. This was nearly as far west as the fire had gone, where the ocean meets the land and the known world ends. Someone lined the stones with care and kept the flame burning against the sea wind, precious and adored, the last hearth before the water. Stand there in the mind's eye, and the feeling is the best one: the fire, the sea, the wind, the stone, all at once. At the edge of everything, we kept the warmth. We always have.
0122.announce: At the edge of the west, a fire verse: The Brittany Hearth.
0122.title: The Brittany Hearth
0122.piece:
Stone-lined, where the west ends,
the hearth the ocean wind befriends.
Three hundred sixty thousand years
of flame, of hopes, of tended fears.
The farthest west the fire had come,
where the Atlantic beats its drum.
Someone lined the stones with care.
Someone kept it burning there.
Precious, kept, adored, the last
before the water, holding fast.
The fire, the sea, the wind, the stone.
We never face the cold alone.
At the edge of the world, we keep
the flame, awake and in our sleep.

0123.event: In Germany, about three hundred fifty thousand years ago, the fossils begin to show heavy brows and stocky bones: the first Neanderthals taking shape in Ice Age Europe. Not yet the classic form, but the direction is clear. The cold's own people were coming: strong, built for winter, made to last through the ice. The dawn was slow, a hundred thousand years of shaping through cold and hunger. Stand in the German cold of that age, and you can see the start of a great people, a work of art in bone and muscle. They would hunt the mammoth and bury their dead. But this was the dawn, and the light was just rising.
0123.announce: A dawn song for the cold-shaped people: The Neanderthal Dawn.
0123.title: The Neanderthal Dawn
0123.piece:
Heavy brows in the morning cold,
the first Neanderthals, strong and bold.
Three hundred fifty thousand years ago,
they faced the ice, they faced the snow.
Stocky bones for the winter's test.
The cold's own people, built the best
for ice. The dawn was slow to break,
a hundred thousand years to make
a people. But the light arose,
and with it, those the winter chose.
They'd hunt the mammoth, brave and true.
They'd bury dead, as we still do.
But this was dawn. The start. The first.
The cold-shaped people quenched their thirst
for life. We sing their morning song.
The dawn has been this clear so long.

0124.event: In Tabun Cave in the Levant, about three hundred forty thousand years ago, the ash lies layer on layer, deep with the keeping of fire through thousands of Levantine winters. Generations of tenders kept it: who, we cannot name, but the continuity is there in the strata, the unbroken line of hands that fed the flame. Sift the ash in the mind's eye, and it is deep with dinners and hopes and fears. The fire is the oldest human truth, and the Tabun hearth is its proof. Someone always stayed to feed it. Someone always will. The flame's the thing that's never-ending, if someone stays.
0124.announce: Ten thousand winters, one flame, a verse: The Tabun Hearth.
0124.title: The Tabun Hearth
0124.piece:
Layer on layer, ash on ash,
the Tabun hearth kept through the clash
of ages. Thousands of winters deep,
the tenders kept it in their keep.
Who kept it? Generations. All
who answered the fire's quiet call.
Three hundred forty thousand years.
The ash is deep with hopes and fears
and dinners. Sift it, and you'll find
the oldest truth of humankind:
the fire we keep will keep us warm.
We kept it through the coldest storm.
The flame's the thing that never ends,
while someone stays, and someone tends.

0125.event: At Kalambo in Zambia, about three hundred thirty thousand years ago, wooden posts and wedges lie at the waterfall's edge: the oldest known woodworking. While the world worked in stone, someone here shaped timber, not for the fire but for form: the post, the wedge, the joint, the true craft of the carpenter before the name existed. Hold a post in the mind's hand, and the maker's ghost stands beside you, patient, skilled, exact. The forest gave more than fuel. It gave building. We worked in wood before we knew the wheel, and the Kalambo timbers sing it: the oldest carpentry, still standing in the mind's eye.
0125.announce: A carpenter's verse from the waterfall: The Kalambo Timbers.
0125.title: The Kalambo Timbers
0125.piece:
Wooden posts by the waterfall,
the oldest carpentry of all.
Three hundred thirty thousand years,
the timber dries the ancient tears
of those who thought that stone alone
could build. The wood has overgrown
that notion. Post and wedge and joint,
the carpenter's first point
of pride. Not for the fire, but form.
The wood stood through the storm
of ages. Hold the post. Feel true
the maker's hand. It reaches you
across the years. The forest gave.
We build. We always were so brave
with wood. The timbers sing it still.
We shape the wood with skill and will.

0126.event: At Olorgesailie in Kenya, about three hundred twenty thousand years ago, volcanic glass lies in the earth that came from quarries far away. It was carried, not found nearby, and the carrying tells the story. Bands may have been trading stone across long distances, and trade would mean more than taking. It means giving, meeting, and the making of relationships in stone. Walk the trade route in the mind's eye, and the newness of it is startling. The glass is sharp with hope, not fear. The Olorgesailie exchange was the start of something we still do: the economy of the heart, measured in miles and trust.
0126.announce: A trader's limerick for the far-carried stone: The Olorgesailie Exchange.
0126.title: The Olorgesailie Exchange
0126.piece:
There once was a band with fine glass
from quarries so far you'd not pass
in a day. But they'd go
through the heat and the snow,
for the trade was the thing with class.
They carried the stone on their backs,
perhaps not for raids, not for fierce attacks,
but to trade and to give,
so that all could live.
Perhaps the first merchants walked those tracks.

0127.event: In the Altai Mountains of Siberia, about three hundred fifteen thousand years ago, the Denisova Cave goes deep, and in its oldest layers lie the first faint traces of the Denisovans: a new kind of human, built for the cold mountains and the far frontier. Not Africa, not Europe, but the east, where the cold air moves out of the cave's dark heart. The traces are faint and old, but they are there, and they say another us lived another history in the high cold. Stand in the Denisova depths in the mind's eye, and the mystery is total. We were not alone. We never were.
0127.announce: A cave-deep verse for the Altai kin: The Denisova Depths.
0127.title: The Denisova Depths
0127.piece:
Deep in the Altai, the cave goes down,
past the dark, past the cold's own crown.
Three hundred fifteen thousand years,
the deepest layers hold the fears
and hopes of a new kind of man,
the Denisovans' ancient plan
for living in the high cold air.
Another us was living there.
Faint traces in the oldest stone.
We were not, are not, alone.
The east had its own history,
its own cold-bloomed mystery.
Stand in the depths and feel it true:
another people. Just like you.

0128.event: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about three hundred ten thousand years ago, skulls with high foreheads and modern faces come out of the desert hillside. They look like us, not quite, but closer than anything before: the brow high, the face flat, the modern shape beginning to show. Stand on that hillside in the mind's eye, and the traces come clear. Look into one of those faces, and you meet your own eyes, almost. Three hundred ten thousand years, and the stream of time narrows. The book of bone has reached the closest chapter yet, and the next page is us.
0128.announce: A mirror poem from the desert hill: The Irhoud Faces.
0128.title: The Irhoud Faces
0128.piece:
High foreheads on the desert hill,
where the ancient wind is still.
Jebel Irhoud, the faces rise,
with almost-modern, knowing eyes.
Three hundred ten thousand years.
They look like us. The past appears
in bone, the closest chapter yet.
I looked, and I will not forget
the moment that the eyes met mine,
across the ages, the design
of us, beginning to show clear.
The modern face is almost here.
The stream of time runs narrow, true.
The next page, reader, is you.

0129.event: At Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about three hundred thousand years ago, the people had long heads and flat faces and brains as large as ours. They are the earliest known Homo sapiens: not yet the glory, not yet the fame, just people, with our brains and our hands, on a desert hillside under the stars. Three hundred thousand years is the start of the story that is still being written, and the seed was them. Look into those skulls in the mind's eye, and there is the first surprise of recognition. Us. At last, us. The first of us did not know they were first. They only lived, and that was enough.
0129.announce: Us, at last, in a naming song: The First of Us.
0129.title: The First of Us
0129.piece:
Long-headed, flat-faced, brains like ours,
beneath the Moroccan stars.
Three hundred thousand years ago,
the first of us began to grow
into the name we'd one day take.
Not for glory. Not for fame's sake.
Just people, on a desert hill,
with hands and hearts and minds, until
the story started, still untold.
The seed was them. The seed was bold.
Look in their eyes and see it true:
at last, at last, it's you.
The first of us. The start. The spring.
We are the song they used to sing
before the words. We sing it still.
We are. We were. We always will.

0130.event: At Olorgesailie in Kenya, about three hundred thousand years ago, the old handaxe's million-year reign comes to an end. Long blades, struck fresh every day from prepared cores, take its place, and the Middle Stone Age begins. It did not happen with a fight. The better tool simply won, the way the better answer always does. Watch the old tradition come undone in the mind's eye, and it feels like watching the world turn. The old ways have their place, and the handaxe earned its million years. But learn the new, or fall behind. The knappers knew. Three hundred thousand years ago, the blade was the future.
0130.announce: The old school falls, in a knapper's verse: The Blade Revolution.
0130.title: The Blade Revolution
0130.piece:
The handaxe had its million years.
Now the long blades, and the cheers
of the knappers for the new way,
fresh-struck blades for every day.
The Middle Stone Age has begun.
The old tradition comes undone,
not with a fight, but with the best
tool winning. Put it to the test:
the blade is the future, keen and bright.
The old school falls without a fight.
At Olorgesailie, the change was seen.
The world turned. The blades were keen.
Learn the new, or fall behind.
The knappers had the stronger mind.
Three hundred thousand years, and true:
the revolution starts with you.

0131.event: At Gademotta in Ethiopia, about three hundred thousand years ago, tiny stone points lie in the earth, made to tip spears. The hunters were arming for distance: throw farther, strike true, and let the point do the work the hand cannot. Hold one up to the light in the mind's eye, and it is small, sharp, perfect. The whirr, the thud, the distant kill. They learned the archer's will before the bow existed: the thrown spear, tipped with stone, could reach where hands alone could never go. Three hundred thousand years ago, the point was the thing, and the hunters practiced until the throwing was true.
0131.announce: Small points, far flight, a hunter's verse: The Gademotta Points.
0131.title: The Gademotta Points
0131.piece:
Tiny points to tip the spear,
for distance, far and near.
Hold one up to the light and see:
small, sharp, perfect, wild and free.
The hunters learned to throw it far,
to strike beneath the distant star
of the hunt. The whirr, the thud.
The point drinks deep. The point draws blood.
Three hundred thousand years, the art
of distance, and the hunter's heart.
Before the bow, the spear was king,
and the tiny point gave it wing.
Practice, throw, retrieve, repeat.
The hunters made the distance sweet.
Small points. Far flight. True aim.
The hunt was never quite the same.

0132.event: At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, about three hundred thousand years ago, shell middens line the Cape coast: the sea's first harvest. Bands of people learned what the ocean gives, prying mussels from the rocks at low tide, and the shore became a menu. Taste the salt in the mind's eye: the iodine, the rich protein, the ancient and faultless food of the tide. The sea provides. The sea is wide. Three hundred thousand years ago, the gatherers learned what the tides teach, and the sea has been feeding us ever since. Walk that shore at low tide, and you are walking the oldest restaurant on earth.
0132.announce: A tide-line song for the shell gatherers: The Pinnacle Point Shells.
0132.title: The Pinnacle Point Shells
0132.piece:
Shell middens on the Cape coast line,
the sea's first harvest, rich and fine.
Pry the mussels from the rock.
The tide comes in. The tide goes back.
Three hundred thousand years, the sea
has fed us. It will ever be
the widest pantry, deep and true.
The gatherers knew what to do:
at low tide, walk the shore and reap
what the ocean's gardens keep.
The salt, the iodine, the feast.
The sea provides, from west to east.
We learned the tides. We learned the song.
The sea has fed us all along.

0133.event: At Qesem in the Levant, about three hundred thousand years ago, flint blades lie in the earth that were resharpened again and again, worn thin with use and love. They were not thrown away. They were kept like treasures, like kin, and the keeper's hands are still on the flint in the mind's eye. Through the clash of ages, the blade stayed: resharpened, true, and kept. It was never just utility. It was care, the bond between the hand and the tool, the keeping. The blades are still there in the earth, waiting. Someone watched the keeper work while the others slept, and learned what keeping means.
0133.announce: A keeper's letter for the well-worn edge: The Kept Blades.
0133.title: The Kept Blades
0133.piece:
My friend, you ask why I keep this blade,
worn thin by every cut I've made.
It is not trash. It is not old.
It is the finest thing I hold.
Resharpened, true, through all the years,
it has known my hopes, my fears.
The flint remembers every hand.
It is the truest in the land.
They tell me: make a new one, friend.
I tell them: this one has no end
while I can keep its edge keen.
The blade and I, we have both seen
three hundred thousand years of use.
We are not done. We will not lose
each other. Keep what you love well.
The kept blade has its tale to tell.

0134.event: In the caves of Europe, about three hundred thousand years ago, Neanderthal children are growing up: big-brained babies needing years of care. The mothers are strong and tender both, nursing the infants through the long slow years the way big brains demand. The nurseries were never rooms. They were the band itself: the circle, the extended hand of kin, the cave, the fire, the mother's arms, the father's hunt. Hold a Neanderthal child in the mind's eye, and the love is ancient and undefiled: the parent's love for the slow-growing young. The oldest lullaby was never written. It was sung, in the cold caves, to us all.
0134.announce: A lullaby from the cold caves: The Neanderthal Nurseries.
0134.title: The Neanderthal Nurseries
0134.piece:
Hush, little one, the cave is warm.
The fire keeps us from the storm.
Big-brained baby, grow up slow.
The years will pass. The love will grow.
Mother's arms and father's hunt,
the band will bear the winter's brunt
for you. Three hundred thousand years,
we've sung away the children's fears.
The nursery is the circle wide,
with kin on every single side.
Sleep, little Neanderthal, sleep deep.
The ancient watch the young ones keep
is love, the oldest, pure and true.
It kept them. It will keep you.
